title: Atlantic -> Trump Ocean?
ticker: BREAKING: Trump says the Atlantic should be renamed "Trump Ocean"
Atlantic covers about 106 million km², roughly one fifth of Earth's surface
After Gulf of America and Mount McKinley, is an ocean next?
Ocean names are coordinated internationally, not set by one country
* This video is a satirical reenactment of a hypothetical scenario
KOWEN NEWS · Today's news, in pixels

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to KOWEN News, today's news in pixels.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: We start tonight with a story that is, quite literally, oceanic in scale.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: President Trump says the Atlantic Ocean needs a new name. And the name he has in mind? Trump Ocean.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Tonight we break it down in three parts.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: First, what exactly was said at the rally. Second, whether anyone can actually rename an ocean. And third, how the rest of the world is reacting.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Let's go straight to our reporter at the rally. What was the mood like out there?

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Thanks. I'm here at a midterm campaign rally, where thousands of supporters packed the arena tonight.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The energy was high from the very beginning, with chants and signs everywhere you looked.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: About halfway through his speech, the president suddenly turned to the subject of the sea.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: He called the Atlantic, quote, a boring name, a very ordinary name. A great ocean, he said, deserves a great name.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Then he added, people come up to me all the time and they say, sir, Trump Ocean sounds so much better.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The crowd erupted, and for a few minutes the arena was chanting Trump Ocean, Trump Ocean.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: After the speech, however, the White House offered no details on any formal plan.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: So was it a joke, or a real proposal? That is already the big debate tonight.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: So what exactly is the ocean the president wants to rename?

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The Atlantic is the second largest ocean on the planet, after the Pacific.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: It covers roughly one hundred and six million square kilometers. That is about one fifth of the Earth's surface.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: To the west, it touches North and South America. To the east, Europe and Africa.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Dozens of countries have an Atlantic coastline. In other words, this is not one nation's ocean.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: If the name ever did change, maps, textbooks and nautical charts around the world would all need to be redrawn.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: This would not be the administration's first attempt at renaming things.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Shortly after taking office in 2025, the president signed an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: North America's tallest peak, Denali, was also given back its old name, Mount McKinley.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Those moves drew sharp criticism at the time, including from the government of Mexico.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: But there is a key difference. Those changes applied to names used by the United States government.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: An entire ocean, shared by many nations, is a completely different matter.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: So who decides what a sea is called? Enter the International Hydrographic Organization, or I H O.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Based in Monaco, the organization publishes the reference guide to the limits and names of the world's oceans and seas.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Changing names there requires discussion and agreement among member states. One country cannot simply decide on its own.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Naming disputes can last for decades. Take the waters between Korea and Japan.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Korea calls it the East Sea, Japan calls it the Sea of Japan, and the two sides have argued over the name on the world stage for years.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: If a single sea can spark a decades long diplomatic fight, most experts say renaming the Atlantic is close to impossible.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Before we hear from the rest of the world, a quick history lesson. Where did the name Atlantic come from in the first place?

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The name Atlantic goes back to ancient Greece. It comes from Atlas, the giant of Greek mythology who was said to hold up the sky.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about the Sea of Atlas around two and a half thousand years ago.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: The Pacific, meanwhile, got its name from the explorer Ferdinand Magellan, who called it the peaceful sea after crossing calm waters in 1520.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: In other words, these names have been on maps for centuries, long before any modern country existed.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Renaming one would mean rewriting not just maps, but a few thousand years of history.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Thanks. Quite a lot of history behind a single name, it turns out.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: So how are people on the other side of the Atlantic taking the news? Let's find out.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: We imagined how people along the Atlantic coast might react. These are hypothetical voices.

lines.speaker: British local
lines.text: We've been sailing across that ocean for centuries. Rename it now? I'd sooner rename tea.

lines.speaker: French fisherman
lines.text: The fish do not care what the ocean is called. Neither do I. Tomorrow I go fishing, same as always.

lines.speaker: Brazilian netizen
lines.text: So can we rename the Amazon the Brazil River? Oh wait, it's already ours.

lines.speaker: Canadian
lines.text: Sorry, well, actually not that sorry, but I'm going to keep calling it the Atlantic.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Online, the parodies are pouring in, as renaming everything in sight becomes the internet's newest game.

scenes.title: JUST FOR FUN: WHAT DO YOU THINK OF TRUMP OCEAN?

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: We also made up a poll, just for fun. To be clear, these are not real survey results.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Absurd came out on top, followed by people who simply see it as a funny joke.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: Only a small minority said they actually like the name.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: We also hit the streets to hear what people think.

lines.speaker: Passerby (M)
lines.text: Honestly, I thought it was fake news at first. Renaming an ocean? Come on.

lines.speaker: Passerby (F)
lines.text: So what's the Pacific going to be called? Trump Ocean two?

lines.speaker: Passerby (M)
lines.text: I mean, I just got used to saying Gulf of America. Now I have to learn a whole new ocean?

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: So how do experts see it?

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.text: Internationally recognized ocean names don't change because one country wants them to. Legally, this would have essentially no effect.

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.text: What the U.S. government can do is use a new name in its own documents, just like it did with the Gulf of America.

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.text: In the end, I'd read this less as a real renaming plan and more as a political message aimed at energizing supporters before the midterms.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.text: That's all from the field. Reporting for KOWEN News.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Let's recap tonight's top story.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: At a midterm rally, President Trump proposed renaming the Atlantic as Trump Ocean. But under international practice, no single country can rename an ocean.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: Around the world, the reaction has been mostly disbelief, along with a flood of parodies.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: And as the East Sea dispute shows, the names on our maps can matter a great deal more than they seem.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: We'll keep watching to see whether this idea sinks or swims.

lines.speaker: Anchor
lines.text: That's it for tonight. This has been KOWEN News, today's news in pixels. Thanks for watching, and good night.
